title: Dynamic length stratifier with kernel-affinity and tail-smooth prefill
creator: Ava Chen
description: Problem: At variable sequence length workloads we see wasted token compute due to padding and suboptimal kernel utilization when batches mix short and long sequences. Objective: implement a runtime stratifier that dynamically forms buckets by sequence-length distribution and steers them to kernels predicted to be most efficient for that bucket, while applying a light-weight tail-smoothing prefill policy to reduce padding amplification without harming latency SLOs. This ticket covers algorithm design, prototype, benchmarks, and a canary rollout to 10% of traffic.
acceptance_criteria: Prototype forms buckets at runtime with <= 5 ms additional scheduling overhead
End-to-end token cost reduced by >= 8% on mixed-length production trace (p95 token cost)
Median and p95 latency SLOs unchanged (within 3% of baseline) for targeted tiers
Scheduler chooses kernel variant per-bucket and logs kernel affinity decisions to telemetry
Graceful fallback path exists: if kernel variant unavailable, route to compatible kernel without causing request failures
technical_design: High-level approach: 1) Observe incoming prefill requests over a short rolling window and compute a lightweight seqlen histogram and quantiles. 2) Use an online cost model to map short/medium/long quantiles to kernel candidates (e.g., 'fused-attn-16' for short, 'sparse-attn-approx' for long) based on historical throughput/latency and current GPU occupancy. 3) Create transient buckets (1-4 buckets per GPU depending on variance) and assign requests with minimal copy/pad. 4) Tail-smooth prefill: for tails (top 2-5% sequence lengths) apply one of two strategies: a) optimistic prefill (start prefill earlier and decode interleaving) or b) length-proxy split (slice long input into prefix prefill + incremental decode) to avoid forcing a whole batch to longest length. 5) Kernel affinity hints are attached to batch metadata and consumed by kernel selector; a verification pass ensures numerical compatibility (dtype, attention pattern). 6) KV cache alignment: ensure bucket assignment preserves KV layout identity; when a request changes bucket across steps, insert a minimal KV remap. 7) Observability: record bucket_id, chosen_kernel, estimated_padding_savings, and prefill_decision in trace metadata. Implementation constraints: keep decision path lock-free and O(1) per request on the hot path; heavy rebalancing runs in background threads. Attention optimizations: prefer flash-attention variants when sequence lengths and memory fit; enable chunked-sparse attention for long tails if model supports it. Kernel selector uses a small feature vector (seq_len, batch_size, current_gpu_mem_frac, model_variant) to score candidates using a pretrained micro-benchmark table updated weekly.
implementation_plan: Phase 1: RFC and simulation (2w) - produce an RFC with simulation against 7 days of production traces, verify theoretical token-cost win. Phase 2: prototype in runtime (3w) - implement stratifier, kernel hinting interface, and tail-smooth prefill policy behind a feature flag. Phase 3: benchmark + perf tuning (2w) - run microbenchmarks across instance types and measure real kernel throughput mapping. Phase 4: telemetry + canary (2w) - enable for 10% of traffic, monitor cost/latency, iterate. Phase 5: rollout (1w) - full rollout with gradual ramp. Deliverables: RFC doc, prototype PR, bench dashboards, canary runbook, rollout playbook.
risks: Incorrect kernel affinity mapping could regress latency for specific models
KV remap overhead might erase padding savings for some traffic patterns
Scheduler complexity exposes new contention points under bursty traffic
Telemetry volume may increase significantly; need sampling and aggregation
notes: Related literature: quantile bucketing for batching (internal whitepaper), incremental prefill ideas from decode interleaving research
Simulator uses anonymized 7-day production trace stored at: gs://redwood-prod-traces/2026-02-week1.gz
